newsitem.title: UK: LIFFE cocoa in late bounce as buy-stops hit.
newsitem.headline: LIFFE cocoa in late bounce as buy-stops hit.

text.p: LIFFE cocoa futures staged a bounce in late Thursday trading on speculative and fund buying as buy-stops were triggered, traders said.
"It's all panic buying by the specs and the funds," said one.
After an uninspiring start, prices were locked in a tight four stg band throughout the morning. But the buying gained momentum in late afternoon after September hit buy stops at 1,125-1,126 stg area.
The contract then motored to close at the day's high of 1,135 stg a tonne, a 17 stg gain, but fell short of matching the one-year peak of 1,140 seen on Monday.
July was also raced higher to the session high of 1,120, up a steep 22 stg on the day. Overall volume was 5,171 lots.
Analysts said September would really need to drop below Tuesday's low 1,097 to spark any real concern, and below 1,065 to negate the bullish move.
But some traders maintained that the rise, which also followed a sharp rebound in New York after Wednesday's setback, was purely technical and was not backed by fundamental factors.
"The market is overbought, overpriced," said a trader at a brokerage firm. "It bears no resemblance to fundamental picture.
One trader valued July, which could come under pressure from fund liquidation ahead of the first delivery day on July 1, at 100 stg below current level.

Others agreed, saying that while the market was building base after last week's rally, a sharp retracement was inevitable if funds liquidate their large long positions. Fundamentally, they argued that concerns over weather-related supply woes were a bit premature.

At the moment, physical supplies in Europe and the United States are ample to meet demand. Traders are awaiting early forecasts of the 1997/98 Ivorian crop but with the current "silly season" in cocoa, they said they could expect a lot of crop rumours.

Early 1997/98 crop estimates vary from a 785,000 tonnes-mark (main crop) by U.S.-based crop analyst Hans Kilian, according to traders, to a more optimistic 1.1 million tonnes for the whole of 1997/98 by Swiss chocolate giant Callebaut Barry, which has two factories in Ivory Coast.
Ivory Coast, the world's largest producer, notched up a record 1.2 million tonnes in 1995/96.
A dry season in July and August which is a strong determinant of the survival rate of pods now setting on trees could be longer than usual if an El Nino weather patterns emerged by then, one said.
